faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Toms River home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. A Pleasant Plains colonial with squirrels at a gable and an Ortley raised house with a winter raccoon tenancy under the floor are both Toms River inspections, and the written quotes differ in almost every line. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Toms River deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. Under the raised shore houses an opossum family is nearly standard equipment by spring, and the screening that ends it has to follow the piling line, not just the skirting. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

Toms River.wildlife_intro:
Toms River is Ocean County's seat and its biggest community, with two distinct halves: the mainland's postwar and newer subdivisions in Silverton, Pleasant Plains, and the Route 37 corridor, and the bay and barrier-island sections, Ortley Beach and the riverfront, where houses sit raised over sand. Mainland calls are squirrels, raccoons, and groundhogs in the subdivisions. Shore-side calls are raccoons and opossums under raised houses, bats in closed seasonal homes, and skunks in the sandy yards. The river and bay keep both halves stocked.

Waterfront houses fight moisture on every front. Crawlspaces on pilings, bulkhead walls, and dock structures give raccoons and opossums dry travel lanes straight to the floor system, and salt air eats vent screens and fasteners years faster than it does inland. Materials matter here: stainless and heavy-gauge mesh, sealed penetrations where pipes pass through the foundation, and caps that survive storm wind. Bats favor the warm, still air under raised houses and inside their roof voids. A shore house proofed with inland materials is a shore house scheduled for a second visit. Toms River work is specified by which half of town the house is in: marine-grade screening and piling details on the water side, canopy and burrow work on the mainland side.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Brick Township attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. In Brick the thumping often starts in a house whose back fence is a bulkhead; the raccoon commuted in along the water and up a corner the land side never shows. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Brick Township lawn at night and it smells like skunk — what is going on?
faqs.a: Neat, cone-shaped holes in turf mean a skunk is mining grubs and earthworms, and late winter adds mating-season scent to the picture. Brick's sandy, grub-rich lawns near the water are skunk cafeterias in the fall, and the cone-holing clusters on the streets closest to the marsh grass. The lasting answer is removing the den site and the food: we clear any skunk sheltering under steps or sheds, screen those voids, and talk through grub-heavy turf, because a lawn full of larvae gets visited nightly no matter how many skunks are taken off it.

Brick Township.wildlife_intro:
Brick Township is a waterfront suburb built along the Metedeconk River and the bay: postwar and newer subdivisions in Herbertsville and Laurelton, lagoon-front homes where every street ends in water, and Forge Pond's woods at the center. Water is never more than a few streets away, and the animals commute along the bulkheads and lagoon banks. Raccoons den in chimneys and under raised sections, opossums and skunks work the low ground, squirrels fill the inland attics, and groundhogs dig the bigger lots near the pond and the river banks.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Brick's lagoon lots give animals a bulkhead highway to the houses, so the inspection here walks the water side first and treats the bulkhead gaps as entries, because they are.
